text: The war between the house of Saul and the house of David dragged on a long time. David grew steadily stronger, while the house of Saul grew steadily weaker.
Sons were born to David in Hebron. His firstborn was Amnon, by Ahinoam of Jezreel;
his second, Kileab, by Abigail the widow of Nabal of Carmel; the third, Absalom, son of Maacah the daughter of Talmai king of Geshur;
the fourth, Adonijah, son of Haggith; the fifth, Shephatiah, son of Abital;
and the sixth, Ithream, by David's wife Eglah. These were born to David in Hebron.
While the war between the house of Saul and the house of David went on, Abner kept strengthening his position in the house of Saul.
Now Saul had a concubine named Rizpah daughter of Aiah. And Ish-bosheth said to Abner, "Why have you slept with my father's concubine?"

Abner was furious at Ish-bosheth's words and said, "Am I a dog's head from Judah? To this very day I have shown loyalty to the house of Saul your father, to his brothers and his friends, and I have not handed you over to David—and now you charge me with an offense over this woman!
May God do so to Abner, and more, if I do not bring about for David exactly what the LORD swore to him:
to take the kingdom from the house of Saul and to establish David's throne over Israel and over Judah, from Dan to Beersheba."
Ish-bosheth could not say another word to Abner, because he was afraid of him.
Then Abner sent messengers on his own behalf to David, saying, "To whom does the land belong? Make a covenant with me, and my hand will be with you to bring all Israel over to you."

versions.text: Then Abner sent messengers on his own behalf to David, saying, "Whose is the land? Make a covenant with me, and my hand will be with you to bring all Israel over to you."
versions.explanation: "Whose is the land?" is cryptic when read aloud; the fuller wording is clearer while remaining literal. A brief footnote explaining that Abner is hinting that David is the rightful ruler of the land would also help the hearer.

versions.text: Then Abner sent messengers on his own behalf to David, saying, "To whom does the land belong?
versions.explanation: The second half of the verse has been dropped: כָּרְתָה בְרִיתְךָ אִתִּי וְהִנֵּה יָדִי עִמָּךְ לְהָסֵב אֵלֶיךָ אֶת־כָּל־יִשְׂרָאֵל ("Make a covenant with me, and behold, my hand will be with you to bring all Israel over to you"). Without it Abner's offer is missing and the closing quotation mark is absent, leaving the sentence unfinished.

text: David answered, "Good. I will make a covenant with you. But I ask one thing of you: do not come into my presence unless you bring Michal daughter of Saul when you come to see me."

versions.text: David answered, "Good. I will make a covenant with you. But I demand one thing of you: do not come into my presence unless you bring Michal daughter of Saul when you come to see me."
versions.explanation: The verb sha'al means "ask/request"; "demand" overstates it, and it also duplicates the word "demand" introduced in verse 14.

text: Then David sent messengers to Ish-bosheth son of Saul with this demand: "Give me my wife Michal, whom I won for myself with a hundred Philistine foreskins."
So Ish-bosheth sent and took her from her husband, Paltiel son of Laish.
Her husband went with her, weeping as he followed her all the way to Bahurim. Then Abner said to him, "Go back home." And he went back.
Abner had also conferred with the elders of Israel, saying, "For some time now you have wanted David as your king.
Now act, for the LORD has said to David, 'By the hand of my servant David I will save my people Israel from the hand of the Philistines and from the hand of all their enemies.'"
Abner spoke to the Benjaminites as well. Then he went to Hebron to tell David everything that Israel and the whole house of Benjamin had agreed to.
When Abner came to David at Hebron with twenty men, David gave a feast for him and his men.

Abner said to David, "Let me go at once and gather all Israel to my lord the king, so that they may make a covenant with you and you may rule over everything your heart desires." So David sent Abner away, and he went in peace.
Just then David's men returned with Joab from a raid, bringing much plunder with them. Abner was no longer with David in Hebron, for David had sent him away, and he had gone in peace.
When Joab and all his troops arrived, he was told, "Abner son of Ner came to the king, and the king sent him away, and he has gone in peace."
So Joab went to the king and said, "What have you done? Abner came to you—why did you let him go? Now he has gotten clean away!
You know Abner son of Ner. He came to deceive you, to learn your movements and everything you are doing."
Then Joab left David and sent messengers after Abner, and they brought him back from the well of Sirah. But David knew nothing about it.

When Abner returned to Hebron, Joab took him aside into the gateway as though to speak with him privately, and there he struck him in the stomach, and he died—in revenge for the blood of Joab's brother Asahel.

versions.text: When Abner returned to Hebron, Joab took him aside into the gateway as though to speak with him privately, and there he struck him in the stomach, and he died—in revenge for the blood of his brother Asahel.
versions.explanation: As written, "his brother Asahel" can be heard as referring to Abner (the nearest antecedent). Naming Joab removes the ambiguity, which matters especially for oral reading.

text: Later, when David heard of it, he said, "I and my kingdom are forever innocent before the LORD of the blood of Abner son of Ner.

May it fall on the head of Joab and on all his father's house! May the house of Joab never be without someone with a running sore or a skin disease, or a man who leans on a staff, or who falls by the sword, or who lacks food."
So Joab and his brother Abishai killed Abner, because he had killed their brother Asahel in the battle at Gibeon.
Then David said to Joab and to all the people with him, "Tear your clothes, put on sackcloth, and walk in mourning before Abner." And King David himself walked behind the bier.
They buried Abner in Hebron, and the king wept aloud at Abner's grave, and all the people wept.
The king sang this lament for Abner: "Should Abner die the death of a fool?

versions.text: The king sang this lament for Abner: "Should Abner die like a fool?
versions.explanation: The Hebrew doubles the root ("die the death of"), which gives the line its lament rhythm; "like a fool" flattens it. A footnote could also note that the word for "fool" (nabal) echoes the name Nabal mentioned in verse 3.

text: Your hands were not bound, your feet were not put in irons. You fell as one who falls before treacherous men." And all the people wept over him again.

versions.text: Your hands were not bound, your feet were not put in irons. You fell as one who falls before the wicked." And all the people wept over him again.
versions.explanation: בְּנֵי־עַוְלָה denotes men of injustice or treachery, not simply "the wicked" in general; "treacherous men" better conveys the murderous deceit of Abner's killers and reads well aloud.

text: Then all the people came to urge David to eat something while it was still day, but David swore, "May God do so to me, and more, if I taste bread or anything else before the sun sets!"
All the people noticed this, and it pleased them; indeed, whatever the king did seemed good to all the people.

versions.text: All the people took note of this and were pleased; indeed, everything the king did pleased them.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew deliberately repeats "in the eyes of all the people," and the verbs are perception verbs ("noticed... seemed good"). Restoring the repetition of "all the people" and the idiom "seemed good" keeps the Hebrew emphasis and gives a fuller cadence for oral reading; "took note of this" is slightly flat and "pleased them" twice in one sentence is repetitive in English.

text: So on that day all the people and all Israel knew that it had not been the king's will to put Abner son of Ner to death.
And the king said to his servants, "Do you not realize that a prince and a great man has fallen in Israel this day?
Today I am weak, though anointed king, and these men, the sons of Zeruiah, are too strong for me. May the LORD repay the evildoer according to his evil!"
